newsitem.title: USA: Boeing airplane market share 64 percent in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Boeing airplane market share 64 percent in 1996.

text.p: Boeing Co. said Tuesday it led the industry in 1996 with a 64 percent share of the market for new commercial airplanes with over 100 seats, driven by demand for its popular 737 airplane.
Boeing said it ended 1996 with 717 announced orders worth $53 billion. About two-thirds of those were for the 737, the world's best-selling airplane.
The company estimated it had net orders in 1996 of 559 airplanes worth $42.8 billion with cancellations and conversions to other airplane models factored out.
Ron Woodard, president of Boeing's Commercial Airplane Group, told reporters at a news conference that demand for the next-generation 737, which rolled out of the factory in December, was strong.
He said Boeing has 517 cumulative orders for the next-generation 737 series, with 3,604 orders for all 737s.

Woodard estimated the Seattle-based company's biggest rival, European consortium Airbus Industrie, had a 32.3 percent market share based on 301 net orders worth about $21.6 billion. He said McDonnell Douglas Corp., which Boeing plans to acquire, had a 3.3 percent share.
"Our customers put us on top again in 1996 because of the superior value of our complete family of airplanes," Woodard said. "Our goal is to remain No. 1."
Woodard reiterated Boeing's goal of reaching a two-thirds market share. The company has historically held about 60 percent of the market and has had a three-year average of about 61 percent.
While 1996 was the company's best year in six or seven years, Woodward said 1997 will be "as good or better than 1996."
He also said he saw a rise in employment in the coming year, although it will be nowhere near as much as 1996's 18,000 new hires.
Woodard predicted 15,900 new airplane orders worth $1.1 trillion over the next 20 years. About 75 percent of that will be new orders, with the balance to replace existing aircraft.
Spurring that growth will be the Asia-Pacific market, he said, adding that that market will define the market size for "stretch" aircraft with 500 or more seats.

Woodard said Boeing and Airbus differ radically in their estimates for the "stretch" market. Boeing estimates potential orders at more than 500 aircraft, while Airbus is hoping the market will provide more than twice that number of orders.
Boeing's largest order in 1996 came from American Airlines, a unit of AMR Corp., for 103 jetliners valued at $6.6 billion, with options on 527 more jets over the next 20 years.
Other major orders included a $4.3 billion order from Continental Airlines Inc. for 78 Next-Generation 737s and a $4 billion order from Malaysia Airlines for 25 wide-body jetliners.
